title: Confinement-Connectivity Coupling Enables High-Efficiency Piezoionic Transduction
summary: Piezoionic hydrogels offer a route to mechanically driven bioelectronic interfaces, but their output is limited by rapid, symmetric ion redistribution that dissipates charge gradients. In biological electrocytes, efficient signal generation arises from the coupling of ion selectivity with spatial confinement that regulates transport. Here, we introduce a confinement-connectivity design strategy for piezoionic hydrogels, implemented through a supramolecular poly(vinyl alcohol)-glycerol-cucurbit[5]uril (PVA-glycerol-CB[5]) mesoporous network with a layered Negative-Neutral-Positive architecture that simultaneously increases pore fraction while reducing characteristic pore size. This architecture constrains ionic redistribution while maintaining a large mobile-ion reservoir, enabling deformation-driven charge separation. Compression generates peak outputs of ~180 mV and ~9 mA and elicits synchronized electromyographic responses in the mouse sciatic nerve without external power. These results establish confinement-connectivity coupling, rather than bulk conductivity, as a materials design framework in which coupling pore connectivity and confinement governs piezoionic transduction.

AI.tldr: A supramolecular PVA–glycerol–CB[5] mesoporous hydrogel with a layered Negative–Neutral–Positive architecture couples increased pore fraction and reduced pore size to constrain ionic redistribution and enable deformation-driven charge separation, producing ~180 mV and ~9 mA on compression and driving electromyographic responses in mouse sciatic nerve without external power.
AI.method: A confinement–connectivity materials-design strategy implemented via a layered mesoporous PVA–glycerol–cucurbit[5]uril (CB[5]) network (Negative–Neutral–Positive layering) that increases pore volume while reducing characteristic pore size to restrict ionic transport; performance assessed by compression-induced electrical output measurements and in vivo electromyographic stimulation of mouse sciatic nerve.
AI.tags: bioelectronics, piezoionic, ion_transport, mesoporous_hydrogel, soft_matter, ionic_conduction, pore_confinement

title: Electrically Tunable Terahertz Chirality from Quantum Geometry
summary: Quantum geometry encoded in the momentum space structure of electronic wavefunctions, governs charge dynamics through Berry curvature, enabling unconventional transport and optical responses. In topological semimetals, this geometry is sampled over Fermi pockets, suggesting electrical control by Fermi surface tuning, yet such control has remained largely limited to DC transport. Here we show that electrostatic gating of the 3D Dirac semimetal Cd3As2 reshapes Fermi pockets surrounding photoinduced Floquet Weyl nodes, enabling electrical control of terahertz (THz) emission chirality. Gate tuning selectively modulates the Berry curvature driven linearly polarized THz component by up to 60% and 49% at positive and negative bias, respectively, while the orthogonal linearly polarized photon-drag component remains unchanged. With the two orthogonal fields intrinsically phase-locked at \sfracπ{2} by the excitation geometry, the selective gate-tuned amplitude control enables the polarization tuning across the Poincaré sphere, achieving near-circular polarization (χ\approx-42°) at +10 V. These results establish Fermi surface tuning as a general route to programmable quantum geometric control of chiral terahertz emission.

AI.tldr: Electrostatic gating of the 3D Dirac semimetal Cd3As2 reshapes Fermi pockets around photoinduced Floquet Weyl nodes to electrically control the chirality of terahertz (THz) emission. Gate tuning selectively modulates the Berry-curvature–driven linearly polarized THz component (up to ≈60% at + bias and 49% at − bias) while leaving the orthogonal photon-drag component unchanged, enabling continuous polarization control on the Poincaré sphere and near-circular emission at +10 V.
AI.method: Experimental: photoexcitation generates Floquet Weyl nodes in Cd3As2; polarization-resolved THz emission spectroscopy combined with electrostatic gating to tune Fermi pockets and isolate Berry-curvature–driven versus photon-drag components; measurement of gate-dependent amplitude and phase to map polarization on the Poincaré sphere.
AI.tags: quantum_geometry, topology, quantum_devices, terahertz, Floquet, Berry_curvature, Dirac_semimetal, gating, Cd3As2

title: Low-Energy Purification of Crystal Defects by Rydberg Excitons
summary: Recent experiments show that optically generated Rydberg excitons in cuprous oxide can neutralize charged impurities, strongly reducing stray electric fields and effectively purifying the crystal. Here, we develop a multichannel theory of Rydberg exciton-impurity scattering that resolves the competing roles of capture, elastic scattering, and inelastic transitions between excitonic states. We find that at high collision energies, as effective under conventional single-photon excitation, purification is reduced relative to Langevin capture. These collisions are accompanied by inelastic redistribution and dominant elastic scattering, including pronounced glory scattering, which suppress purification efficiency. We identify a quantum regime at ultralow collision energies favorable for purification, where only the s-wave contributes: capture is enhanced while elastic and inelastic channels are strongly suppressed. This regime can be accessed via degenerate two-photon excitation of even-parity Rydberg excitons with tunable recoil, additionally enabling the systematic exploration of exciton-impurity scattering over a wide range of collision energies beyond what is readily achievable in atomic counterparts in atomic gas experiments.

AI.tldr: Multichannel quantum scattering theory for Rydberg exciton–impurity collisions in Cu2O shows that high collision energies (typical single-photon excitation) reduce impurity neutralization because elastic (including glory) and inelastic channels dominate over capture; an ultralow-energy s-wave quantum regime—accessible via degenerate two-photon excitation of even‑parity Rydberg excitons with tunable recoil—enhances capture and purification by suppressing elastic and inelastic processes.
AI.method: Developed a multichannel exciton–impurity scattering theory that separates capture, elastic scattering, and inelastic excitonic transitions; analyzed energy-dependent cross sections and compared to Langevin capture limits; proposed experimental access to the ultralow s‑wave regime via degenerate two‑photon excitation with tunable recoil.
AI.tags: impurity_scattering,Rydberg_excitons,inelastic_scattering,Langevin_capture,s-wave_regime,two-photon_excitation,glory_scattering

title: Mobile Exceptional Points Generate Momentum-Space Switching Domains
summary: Exceptional points (EPs), non-Hermitian degeneracies where both eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce, play a central role in the topology of non-Hermitian spectra. Recent advances have enabled the controlled creation and manipulation of EPs in a wide range of physical systems, raising the question of what new band topology emerges when EPs become mobile under cyclic modulation. Here we show that mobile EPs generate momentum-space switching domains that partition the Brillouin zone into regions with distinct band-switching behavior. Using a minimal two-band lattice model, we introduce a band-permutation invariant that determines whether eigenmodes exchange after one modulation cycle. The boundaries between switching regions arise from the projection of EP trajectories in an extended parameter space combining crystal momentum and the modulation parameter. As the modulation strength increases, the switching domains expand and eventually cover the entire Brillouin zone, resulting in global band switching. The predicted switching-domain structure is further demonstrated in a photonic crystal with lossy materials. These results open a new avenue within non-Hermitian topology by enabling the engineering of EP-driven phenomena through their controlled motion.

AI.tldr: Mobile exceptional points in non-Hermitian two-band lattices partition the Brillouin zone into momentum-space ‘‘switching domains’’ whose regions exhibit distinct band-permutation (eigenmode-exchange) after a cyclic modulation; domain boundaries are projections of EP trajectories in an extended (k + modulation) parameter space, and increasing modulation strength expands domains to produce global band switching. The phenomenon is illustrated in a lossy photonic-crystal implementation.
AI.method: Construct a minimal two-band lattice model and define a band-permutation invariant to diagnose whether eigenmodes exchange after one modulation cycle; analyze EP trajectories in an extended parameter space combining crystal momentum and the modulation parameter to find projected boundaries between switching domains; demonstrate the predicted switching-domain structure in a photonic crystal with lossy materials.
AI.tags: topology, exceptional_points, non-Hermitian, band_permutation, Brillouin_zone, photonic_crystal, band_topology

title: Superconductivity-Enabled Conversion of Ferromagnetic Resonance into Standing Spin Waves
summary: Superconductors can transport spin without Joule dissipation, yet their coherent coupling to short-wavelength magnons in insulating magnets remains largely unexplored. Here we demonstrate experimentally and theoretically that a conventional diffusive superconductor can enable the conversion of the uniform ferromagnetic-resonance (FMR) mode into perpendicular standing spin waves (PSSWs) in an adjacent ferrimagnetic insulator. In Bi-substituted iron-garnet/Nb bilayers, the microwave transmission develops an additional resonance feature that appears only below the Nb transition temperature and lies close to the uniform FMR peak. A microscopic theory that self-consistently couples the quasiclassical Keldysh--Usadel description of the superconducting condensate to the Landau--Lifshitz--Gilbert dynamics shows that the conversion requires two ingredients: (i) an interfacial spin-transfer torque mediated by spin-polarized triplet Cooper pairs and (ii) a depth-dependent effective field produced by Abrikosov vortices (electromagnetic proximity). The resulting susceptibility reproduces the measured lineshapes and establishes superconductivity as an active control knob for exchange standing-wave modes in magnetic insulators.

AI.tldr: Experimental and theoretical demonstration that a diffusive superconducting Nb layer converts the uniform ferromagnetic-resonance (FMR) mode in an adjacent Bi-substituted iron-garnet into perpendicular standing spin waves (PSSWs) below the superconducting transition. The effect appears as an extra microwave-transmission resonance near the FMR peak and is explained by (i) interfacial spin-transfer torque from spin-polarized triplet Cooper pairs and (ii) a depth-dependent effective field from Abrikosov vortices (electromagnetic proximity). A self-consistent Keldysh–Usadel + Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert theory reproduces the observed lineshapes.
AI.method: Combined experiment (microwave transmission on Bi-substituted iron-garnet/Nb bilayers showing a Tc-dependent additional resonance) and microscopic theory that self-consistently couples the quasiclassical Keldysh–Usadel description of the superconducting condensate to Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert magnetization dynamics; identifies spin-polarized triplet-mediated interfacial torque and vortex-induced depth-dependent field as the necessary ingredients.
AI.tags: superconductivity,vortex,ferromagnetic_resonance,PSSW,triplet_Cooper_pairs,spin-transfer_torque,Keldysh-Usadel,Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert,electromagnetic_proximity,BiIG/Nb

title: Curvature-induced nonlinear anomalous Hall effect in thin magnetic shells
comment: main text: 11 pages, 4 figures; supplementary inf. 6 pages 6 figures
summary: Optoelectronic and nonlinear transport experiments probe the quantum geometric tensor of Bloch states, whose real and imaginary components -- the quantum metric and the Berry curvature -- are typically constrained by symmetry. Here, we show that geometric bending provides a route to engineer such responses in centrosymmetric ferromagnets. Curvature-induced strain gradients across the shell thickness break inversion symmetry and activate an orbital Rashba coupling. In the presence of in-plane magnetization and spin-orbit coupling, this generates spin textures with a nontrivial quantum geometry, leading to an intrinsic nonlinear anomalous Hall effect (NAHE) governed by the quantum metric and maximized when the magnetization aligns with the applied electric field. When geometric deformations further break twofold rotational symmetry around the out-of-plane axis, an additional NAHE emerges, maximal for magnetization perpendicular to the driving electric field and governed by the Berry curvature dipole, thus giving access to the imaginary component of the quantum geometric tensor. These results establish curved ferromagnetic shells as a platform for engineering anisotropic nonlinear transport and for selectively probing both components of the quantum geometric tensor.

AI.tldr: Curvature in centrosymmetric ferromagnetic shells produces strain-gradient–induced orbital Rashba coupling which, together with spin–orbit coupling and magnetization, generates spin textures with nontrivial quantum geometry. This yields intrinsic nonlinear anomalous Hall responses: a quantum-metric–governed NAHE maximal when magnetization aligns with the electric field, and, when further symmetry is broken, a Berry-curvature-dipole–driven NAHE maximal for magnetization perpendicular to the field. Curved ferromagnetic shells are thus proposed as a platform to engineer anisotropic nonlinear transport and selectively probe both components of the quantum geometric tensor.
AI.method: Theoretical/analytical modeling of curved ferromagnetic shells incorporating curvature-induced strain gradients (activating orbital Rashba), spin–orbit coupling and magnetization; calculation of resulting spin textures, quantum geometric tensor (quantum metric and Berry curvature dipole) and prediction of intrinsic nonlinear anomalous Hall effects under different symmetry-breaking scenarios.
AI.tags: quantum_geometry,Berry_curvature,quantum_metric,nonlinear_anomalous_Hall,orbital_Rashba,spin-orbit_coupling,curved_ferromagnets,strain_gradient,quantum_devices

title: Phase Stability of Superfluid $^{3}\mathrm{He}$ in Anisotropic Aerogel
summary: The A and B phases of superfluid 3 He have vector degrees of freedom that reflect their characteristic broken symmetries, respectively chiral and spin-orbit rotation axes. Anisotropic disorder in the superfluid, imbibed in uniformly strained silica aerogel, orients these degrees of freedom, thereby affecting phase stability. These degrees of freedom have been found to spontaneously reorient at a field-independent transition temperature Tx , that can be accounted for with a temperature dependent anisotropic Ginzburg-Landau model.

AI.tldr: Vector order-parameter axes in the A and B phases of superfluid 3He are oriented by anisotropic disorder introduced by uniformly strained silica aerogel; these orientations, which influence phase stability, show a field-independent spontaneous reorientation at a transition temperature Tx that is reproduced by a temperature-dependent anisotropic Ginzburg–Landau model.
AI.method: Observation of disorder-induced orientation and spontaneous reorientation of vector degrees of freedom in 3He imbibed into uniformly strained silica aerogel, analyzed with a phenomenological temperature-dependent anisotropic Ginzburg–Landau theory to account for the field-independent Tx.
AI.tags: superfluid_He3, anisotropic_disorder, aerogel, Ginzburg-Landau, phase_transition, order_parameter, superconducting_impurity

title: Quantum Scalar Spin Chirality in Coplanar Kagome Antiferromagnets
summary: We theoretically demonstrate that quantum fluctuations inherent to antiferromagnets can generate scalar spin chirality at zero temperature even in coplanar ordered magnets. In a kagome antiferromagnet with coplanar ground-state spin configurations, the quantum-fluctuation-induced scalar spin chirality is shown to arise at zero temperature when an effective time-reversal-like antiunitary symmetry is broken in the Hamiltonian describing fluctuations, and a magnetic point group of the classical ground state allows for its presence. The scalar spin chirality fluctuations are shown to grow further with increasing temperature by thermally excited magnons. These scalar spin chirality fluctuations can reach a magnitude comparable to the static one predicted for noncoplanar spin structures, highlighting their physical implications in coplanar spin systems.

AI.tldr: Quantum fluctuations in a coplanar kagome antiferromagnet can produce a nonzero scalar spin chirality at T=0 when an effective time-reversal–like antiunitary symmetry of the fluctuation Hamiltonian is broken and the magnetic point group permits it; thermal magnons further enhance these chirality fluctuations to magnitudes comparable to static noncoplanar cases.
AI.method: Theoretical symmetry-based analysis and calculation of quantum and thermal magnon fluctuation contributions to scalar spin chirality in a kagome antiferromagnet (analytical/model study of the fluctuation Hamiltonian and magnetic point-group constraints).
AI.tags: topology, quantum_geometry, antiferromagnet, kagome_lattice, magnons, scalar_spin_chirality, symmetry_analysis

title: Magnetic Quantum Criticality inside the Superconducting State Revealed by Penetration Depth Scaling with Local $T_{\mathrm c}$
summary: We demonstrate a magnetic quantum critical point embedded within the superconducting state of Zn-doped CeCoIn$_5$, revealed by a pronounced peak in the magnetic penetration depth at zero temperature $λ(0)$. Using scanning SQUID microscopy, we determine the local superconducting transition temperature $T_{\mathrm c}$ and $λ(0)$. By parameterizing $λ(0)$ in terms of the local $T_{\mathrm c}$ rather than nominal Zn substitution, we circumvent the ambiguity caused by doping inhomogeneity and enable a more precise extraction of the critical exponent. The extracted exponent exceeds the clean spin-density-wave value, indicating a disorder-modified quantum critical regime. The enhancement of $λ(0)$ reflects the suppression of the superfluid stiffness and is consistent with critical scaling. Our approach provides a route to uncover intrinsic quantum critical behavior hidden by inhomogeneity in unconventional superconductors.

AI.tldr: A magnetic quantum critical point lies inside the superconducting phase of Zn-doped CeCoIn5, revealed by a pronounced peak in the zero-temperature magnetic penetration depth λ(0). By correlating locally measured λ(0) with local Tc using scanning SQUID microscopy, the authors remove effects of doping inhomogeneity and extract a critical exponent larger than the clean spin-density-wave value, implying a disorder-modified quantum critical regime with suppressed superfluid stiffness consistent with critical scaling.
AI.method: Local scanning SQUID microscopy to map superconducting transition temperature Tc and magnetic penetration depth λ(0), parameterization of λ(0) as a function of local Tc to avoid nominal-doping inhomogeneity, and extraction of the quantum-critical exponent from the scaling of λ(0) (and inferred superfluid stiffness) compared to clean spin-density-wave expectations.
AI.tags: superconducting_impurity,quantum_criticality,scanning_SQUID,penetration_depth,superfluid_stiffness,disorder

title: Size-Limited Room Temperature Single-Photon Emission from Sidewall-Treated Fractional Dimension InGaN Quantum Dots: Determined by Density-of-States-Corrected Ultrafast Carrier Dynamics and Improved Signal-to-Noise Ratio
summary: Room-temperature single-photon emission (SPE) resulting from a biexciton-exciton cascaded decay is demonstrated for the first time from chemically and photoelectrochemically etched site-controlled In0.14Ga0.86N quantum dots (QDs) embedded in vertical GaN nanowires. Diameter-dependent biexciton-exciton dynamics are analysed to determine the eligibility of QD as a single-photon emitter. The signal-to-noise ratio degrades with increasing QD diameter. Background noise photons pose a bottleneck to achieving SPE. This is also explained from a carrier dynamics perspective. Surface recombination contributes to inhomogeneous broadening at QD diameters larger than 35 nm. Below 35 nm, density-of-states-corrected Auger gradually becomes the principal biexciton-decay route with further reduction in QD diameter, thereby quenching the possibility of thermal broadening and setting a threshold for SPE. Below 9 nm, the Auger recombination rate becomes manyfold of other decay rates, causing multi-photon suppression via single Auger decay to form an exciton. Surface recombination probability of this exciton is minimized while biexciton state filling probability is maximized by reducing sidewall surface states through wet-treatment. These improve biexciton state preparation and enhance the single-photon purity of the exciton towards the exciton Bohr radius (3 nm) regime. Far away from this regime, higher-order autocorrelations to characterize quantum emission involving multi-photon events are discussed. This study establishes a generalized physical framework for predetermining SPE probability as a function of QD surface and geometry down to the exciton Bohr radius regime, with practical implementations. This work shows the pathway to design and develop next-generation semiconductor QDs for high-purity room-temperature SPE.

AI.tldr: Demonstrates room-temperature single-photon emission from chemically and photoelectrochemically etched, site-controlled In0.14Ga0.86N quantum dots embedded in vertical GaN nanowires via a biexciton→exciton cascade. The study maps how QD diameter controls biexciton–exciton dynamics and identifies competing channels—surface recombination and density-of-states-corrected Auger—setting size thresholds: above ≈35 nm surface recombination broadens emission, between ≈35 nm and ≈9 nm DOS-corrected Auger increasingly dominates biexciton decay, and below ≈9 nm very fast Auger suppresses multi-photon events enabling high single-photon purity. Wet chemical sidewall treatment reduces surface states, improving biexciton preparation and SPE purity; higher-order autocorrelations for multi-photon characterization are discussed.
AI.method: Fabrication of site-controlled In0.14Ga0.86N QDs inside vertical GaN nanowires by chemical and photoelectrochemical etching, followed by diameter-dependent experimental analysis of biexciton–exciton dynamics and carrier-recombination processes. Interpretation uses carrier-dynamics arguments including surface-recombination effects and density-of-states-corrected Auger recombination; sidewall wet-treatment is applied to reduce surface states; photon-correlation (autocorrelation) metrics are used to evaluate single-photon purity.
AI.tags: quantum_devices, quantum_dots, single-photon_emission, biexciton-exciton, Auger_recombination, surface_recombination, GaN_nanowires, room-temperature_SPE

title: Critical temperatures and critical currents of wide and narrow quasi-one-dimensional superconducting aluminum structures in zero magnetic field
summary: We measured the critical temperatures and critical switching and retrapping currents of wide and narrow thin-film quasi-one-dimensional superconducting aluminum structures of the same thickness in zero magnetic field. For the first time, we found that the narrower the structure, the lower the critical temperature and critical current density in the structure. Probably, the influence of depairing centers that are on dirty longitudinal boundaries of the structure, is the stronger than the narrower the structure. It is found for the first time that, in most cases, the temperature-dependent switching critical current in both structures is approximated by two functions. At temperatures below the temperature corresponding to the bottom of the resistive N-S transition of structures, the switching critical current is described by the Kupriyanov-Lukichev theory. At temperatures close to the top of the N-S transition, the switching current is linear with temperature and coincides with the critical Josephson current. At these temperatures, Josephson SNS junctions are formed in structures.

AI.tldr: Experimental transport study of thin-film quasi-1D Al structures finds that narrower wires show suppressed Tc and critical current density; switching current vs T separates into two regimes — Kupriyanov–Lukichev behaviour at low T and a linear, Josephson SNS-like critical current near the top of the N–S transition — attributed to depairing centers at dirty longitudinal boundaries and formation of SNS junctions near Tc.
AI.method: Low-temperature electrical transport measurements of critical temperatures, switching and retrapping currents in wide and narrow thin-film quasi-one-dimensional aluminum structures (zero magnetic field), with comparison to Kupriyanov–Lukichev theory and identification of Josephson SNS behavior near the N–S transition.
AI.tags: superconductivity, superconducting_impurity, thin_films, quasi-one-dimensional, critical_current, SNS_junctions, Kupriyanov-Lukichev, transport_measurements, aluminum

title: Spin-orbit interaction in core-shell semiconductor-metal nanowires
summary: We study theoretically the spin-orbit interaction of electrons confined in a tubular semiconductor nanowire, between an inner semiconductor core and an outer metallic extra shell. A band off-offset potential is present at the inner semiconductor-semiconductor interface and a more complex potential barrier at the outer metal-semiconductor contact. The cross section of the nanowire has a hexagonal geometry. We use a model derived from the k-dot-p method, and discuss the effects of the interface potentials on the strength of the spin-orbit coupling and on the localization of the wave functions within the semiconductor shell

AI.tldr: The paper models spin–orbit coupling in a tubular semiconductor nanowire (hexagonal cross section) with an inner semiconductor core and outer metallic shell, showing how a band offset at the inner interface and a metal–semiconductor barrier at the outer contact modify the SO coupling strength and the spatial localization of shell states.
AI.method: A k·p-derived theoretical model for a hexagonal core–shell nanowire including band-offset and metal–semiconductor interface potentials; analysis of resulting spin–orbit coupling strength and electron wavefunction localization within the semiconductor shell.
AI.tags: spin_orbit, semiconductor_nanowire, k_dot_p, interface_potential, wavefunction_localization, hexagonal_cross_section, quantum_devices, quantum_geometry

title: Shift of the maxima of the critical currents of different polarity relative to the zero magnetic flux along the flux axis in a superconducting asymmetric aluminum ring
summary: We measured the rectification of an ac voltage in a structure of superconducting circularly-asymmetric aluminum rings in series, permeated with a magnetic flux and biased with a low-frequency alternating current (without a dc component). This rectification is due to the shift of the maxima of the critical currents of different polarity relative to the zero flux in opposite directions along the flux axis in the asymmetric ring. For the first time, we propose a model for a temperature-dependent phase shift equal to difference between dimensionless kinetic inductances of wide and narrow semirings having the same length and thickness. The shift is not zero in the case of different critical currents densities in both semirings. This is possible only in a situation of different critical temperatures of both semirings. The model describes well the temperature-dependent shift of the maxima of the critical currents, answers the long-standing mysterious challenge of the shift and removes extremely strange contradiction between the results of different measurements, previously found in circularly-asymmetric aluminum structures.

AI.tldr: Measured rectification of an AC bias in series circularly–asymmetric aluminum rings is attributed to a flux-dependent shift of opposite-polarity critical-current maxima. The authors introduce a temperature-dependent phase-shift model given by the difference of dimensionless kinetic inductances of the wide and narrow semirings (same length/thickness) that requires differing critical temperatures; the model quantitatively reproduces the observed temperature-dependent shifts and resolves prior experimental contradictions.
AI.method: Low-frequency AC rectification measurements on series-connected, circularly asymmetric Al rings under applied magnetic flux, combined with a phenomenological/theoretical model that identifies the phase shift as the difference in dimensionless kinetic inductances between wide and narrow semirings (incorporating differing critical current densities and critical temperatures) and comparison of model predictions to the temperature dependence of critical-current maxima positions.
AI.tags: superconductivity,kinetic_inductance,asymmetric_rings,flux_quantization,rectification,phase_shift,temperature_dependence,aluminum

title: Spin-coherence characterization of boron vacancy defects in hexagonal boron nitride with broadband microwave pulses
summary: Negatively charged boron vacancy (VB-) defects in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) are promising for nanoscale-proximity quantum sensing. To evaluate their performance, it is important to characterize the spin coherence times T2* and T2. In this study, we realized sub-GHz Rabi oscillations of VB- using an isotopically enriched hBN thin film directly stamped onto a narrow gold wire. Using these strong microwave pulses, we performed Ramsey interference and Hahn echo measurements. The Ramsey interference signal showed Gaussian-like decay, yielding T2* = 13.8 ns. The Hahn echo measurement gave T2 = 108.7 ns and a stretch factor of α= 1.25. These results experimentally clarify the spin coherence properties of VB- and provide an effective method for evaluating the coherence of spin defects in van der Waals thin films with broad resonance linewidths.

AI.tldr: Pulse-EPR study of negatively charged boron-vacancy (VB-) centers in isotopically enriched hBN: sub-GHz Rabi driving with an hBN film on a narrow gold wire yields Ramsey T2* = 13.8 ns (Gaussian decay) and Hahn-echo T2 = 108.7 ns with stretch factor α = 1.25, providing an experimental characterization and a practical method for assessing coherence in vdW thin films with broad linewidths.
AI.method: Experimental pulsed microwave spin resonance: isotopically enriched hBN thin film directly stamped onto a narrow gold wire to enable strong (sub-GHz) Rabi driving; performed Ramsey interference (extracting T2*) and Hahn-echo measurements (extracting T2 and stretch factor).
AI.tags: quantum_devices, quantum_sensing, spin_defects, boron_vacancy, van_der_Waals, isotope_enriched, Rabi_oscillations, Ramsey, Hahn_echo, coherence_times

title: Unusual critical currents in quasi-one-dimensional superconducting aluminum two-width structures in a magnetic field
summary: We measured unusual critical currents as functions of temperature in the zero field and as functions of a magnetic field perpendicular to the substrate surface at a given temperature close to the critical temperature in thin-film long quasi-one-dimensional superconducting aluminum two-width structures consisting of narrow and wide wires with different critical temperatures. It is found that the experimental critical switching current as a function of the field at a given temperature, determined by the appearance of a dc voltage on a short section of the structure, is nonlocal (dependent on electron transport in the area containing the junction line between the narrow and wide wires). When current flows through the narrow and wide wires of the structure, the switching currents, experimental and calculated within the framework of the Ginzburg-Landau theory, differ radically from each other. A nonzero switching current exists in high fields greater than the maximum critical magnetic field in a quasi-one-dimensional superconducting wire. In the aluminum two-width structures studied here, the unusual measured switching current challenges description by known theories.

AI.tldr: Measured anomalous switching currents in thin-film quasi-1D aluminum two-width (narrow+wide) wires: switching current vs perpendicular field shows nonlocal dependence tied to the junction between widths, persists above the nominal critical field, and deviates strongly from Ginzburg–Landau predictions—challenging existing theory.
AI.method: Experimental transport measurements of critical (switching) current as functions of temperature and perpendicular magnetic field near Tc in long quasi-1D thin-film Al two-width structures; switching identified via onset of a dc voltage on a short segment; results compared against calculations within Ginzburg–Landau theory.
AI.tags: superconductivity,quasi-one-dimensional,thin-film,nonlocal_effects,Ginzburg-Landau_comparison,vortex_physics,critical_current,aluminum

title: Transport Detection of Whirlpools in GaAs Electron Liquid
summary: We report the formation of large-scale steady-state whirlpools in a GaAs-based two-dimensional electron liquid and demonstrate them by straightforward transport measurements. A whirlpool forming inside a circular cavity adjoining a wide conducting channel appears as a negative four-terminal resistance over a broad range of temperatures and cavity sizes. The effect scales with the Gurzhi length, in quantitative accord with the hydrodynamic analogy. Obtained results firmly establish this analogy and probe the limits of its applicability.

AI.tldr: Observation of large-scale steady-state electron whirlpools (hydrodynamic vortices) in a GaAs two-dimensional electron liquid, manifested as negative four-terminal resistance in a circular cavity connected to a wide channel; the effect persists across temperatures and cavity sizes and scales quantitatively with the Gurzhi length, validating the hydrodynamic analogy and probing its limits.
AI.method: Mesoscopic transport experiments on a GaAs 2D electron gas: four-terminal resistance measurements in devices with a circular cavity adjoining a wide conducting channel; analyze sign and scaling of nonlocal resistance versus cavity size and temperature and compare to hydrodynamic (Gurzhi-length) predictions.
AI.tags: vortex, hydrodynamic_electrons, Gurzhi_length, nonlocal_transport, GaAs_2DEG

title: Local probing of superconductivity at oxide interfaces with atomic force microscopy
summary: Superconductivity in strontium titanate has remained enigmatic for more than 50 years. The LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ (LAO/STO) heterointerface enables systematic dimensional confinement, from a two-dimensional electron gas to quasi-one-dimensional nanostructures, providing access to this quantum state. Transport measurements in patterned devices reveal puzzling phenomena, including width-independent critical currents and anomalous pairing suggestive of one-dimensional behavior, but direct local probes of the patterned interface and its superconducting response have been lacking. Here we use ultralow-temperature non-contact atomic force microscopy, dissipation spectroscopy, and Kelvin probe force microscopy to locally probe signatures of superconductivity in patterned LAO/STO devices. Spatially resolved energy-dissipation measurements reveal superconducting signatures, with features confined in some devices to edge channels approximately 200 nm wide. Dissipation spectra exhibit a characteristic nonlinear bias dependence that provides a local diagnostic of superconductivity, consistent with the intermediate carrier-density regime near the superconducting dome, and persisting up to the critical field. These results establish atomic force microscopy as a local probe of superconductivity in patterned LAO/STO structures and provide a route to addressing longstanding questions about quantum confinement and transport anomalies in correlated oxide nanostructures.

AI.tldr: Ultralow-temperature non-contact AFM, dissipation spectroscopy, and Kelvin probe force microscopy directly detect superconducting signatures at patterned LaAlO3/SrTiO3 interfaces. Spatially resolved dissipation maps reveal superconductivity confined in some devices to ~200 nm edge channels; dissipation spectra show a nonlinear bias dependence consistent with an intermediate carrier-density regime near the superconducting dome and persist up to the critical field. The work establishes AFM-based local probes for addressing quantum confinement and anomalous transport in oxide nanostructures.
AI.method: Ultralow-temperature non-contact atomic force microscopy combined with spatially resolved energy-dissipation spectroscopy and Kelvin probe force microscopy on patterned LAO/STO heterointerfaces; analysis of dissipation spectra versus bias and magnetic field to identify and spatially resolve superconducting response (edge-channel confinement ~200 nm).
AI.tags: superconductivity,oxide_heterostructures,LAO/STO,AFM,dissipation_spectroscopy,edge_channels,quantum_confinement,nanoscale_superconductivity,quantum_devices

title: Theory of quantum decoherence in macroscopic topological insulators
summary: Quantum decoherence-the loss of quantum coherence due to interactions with an environment-plays a central role in quantum transport, and controlling this ubiquitous yet inevitable phenomenon is essential for practical quantum technologies. Despite its importance, the microscopic mechanisms of decoherence in infinite-size topological insulators remain poorly understood. Here, we develop a comprehensive theory that quantitatively investigates how quantum decoherence shapes the quantum spin Hall effect in macroscopic topological insulators, and reveal that decoherence-induced corrections scale quadratically with impurity density. Besides, we uncover a previously unidentified mechanism of the extrinsic spin Hall effect: a second-order skew-scattering process intrinsically tied to quantum decoherence-fundamentally distinct from, yet substantially stronger than, the conventional third-order skew-scattering mechanism. Furthermore, we predict a new scaling law in which the decoherence-induced spin Hall conductivity scales quadratically with the longitudinal conductivity, providing a clear experimental signature of decoherence effects. Our results establish the essential role of decoherence in quantum transport of topological insulators and reveal that macroscopic topological insulators offer a promising platform for next-generation spintronic applications.

AI.tldr: Develops a microscopic transport theory showing quantum decoherence controls the quantum spin Hall effect in infinite-size topological insulators: decoherence-induced corrections scale ~n_imp^2 and produce a novel second-order skew‑scattering extrinsic spin Hall mechanism stronger than conventional third‑order skew scattering; predicts spin Hall conductivity ∝ (longitudinal conductivity)^2 as an experimental signature.
AI.method: Analytical microscopic transport theory for macroscopic (infinite-size) topological insulators incorporating decoherence and impurity scattering; perturbative scattering analysis identifies decoherence-induced second‑order skew‑scattering and derives scaling laws for spin Hall and longitudinal conductivities.
AI.tags: topology,quantum_decoherence,spin_Hall,skew_scattering,impurity_scattering,transport,spintronics

title: Enhancement of superconducting stiffness in hybrid superconducting-metallic bilayers
summary:
Boosting superconductivity by metallic reservoirs is the essence of Kivelson's bilayer proposal.
  One layer provides pairing to the electrons, while the weakly coupled metal provides additional phase coherence to those pairs by mediating extended-range pair-pair coupling.
  Demonstrating significant and unambiguous performance gains with strong-coupling methods for such set-ups had been difficult.
  In the present work, we study these systems doped away from half-filling, corresponding to a partially spin-polarized 1D Anderson- or Kondo-lattice.
  We show that this breaks the coexistence of dominant superconducting and density-density correlations decisively in favour or the former.
  Consequently, we provide evidence that in this doped regime, superconducting near-long-range order is not precluded by a small charge-gap in the thermodynamic limit, as we have recently shown to be the case at half-filling [JE Ebot $et$ $al.$, arXiv:2602.11153 [cond-mat.supr-con]].
  We study the complex manner in which the enhancement of superconductivity in the pairing layer depends on the parameters of the metal, and especially that both pairing-limited and stiffness-limited regimes may appear in these systems.
  In addition to superconducting bilayers, our results are relevant, via a particle-hole transformation, for heavy-fermion Kondo-lattice materials in magnetic fields, as we provide previously lacking insight on the competition between antiferromagnetic and easy-plane magnetism, as well as a route for comprehensive indirect tests of Kivelson's bilayer proposal well beyond previous capabilities.

AI.tldr: Doping Kivelson-style bilayer systems away from half-filling (mapped to a partially spin-polarized 1D Anderson- or Kondo-lattice) decisively suppresses competing density correlations and promotes dominant superconducting correlations. The authors find that near-long-range superconducting order survives despite a small thermodynamic charge gap found at half-filling, and that enhancement of pairing in the superconducting layer depends sensitively on metal parameters, exhibiting both pairing-limited and stiffness-limited regimes. Via a particle–hole mapping the results also inform competition between antiferromagnetic and easy-plane magnetism in heavy-fermion Kondo-lattice systems and provide routes to test Kivelson’s bilayer proposal.
AI.method: Model study of doped, partially spin-polarized 1D Anderson- and Kondo-lattice bilayers using many-body analysis of correlation functions and charge-gap scaling to identify dominant superconducting versus density correlations and characterize parameter-dependent pairing/stiffness regimes (theoretical/numerical study).
AI.tags: superconductivity, superconducting_impurity, Kondo_lattice, Anderson_lattice, heavy_fermion, bilayer, doping, antiferromagnetism, easy-plane_magnetism, phase_coherence

title: Compressibility of micromagnetic solutions in tensor train format
summary: For three-dimensional (3D) magnetic objects with linear size $L$ exceeding a few exchange lengths, the micromagnetic state exhibits pronounced informational sparsity: low-dimensional, high-gradient regions (e.g., domain walls) coexist with near-uniformly magnetized volumetric domains. Because standard micromagnetic simulation methods discretize the magnetization on near-uniform 3D grids with linear cell size $a$, they cannot take advantage of this sparsity. The computational problem scales as $\sim L^3$ and $\sim (1/a)^3$. In this Letter, we establish that direct tensor-train (TT) representations overcome these poor scalings by exploiting the spatial sparsity optimally, while preserving accuracy in a controlled way. Focusing on representative flux-closure configurations in soft-magnetic rectangular prisms, in the near-micrometer regime, we demonstrate that the parameter count of TT-compressed micromagnetic data scales approximately as $L^{1.8}$ and $(1/a)^{1.2}$. Hence the relative advantage over dense discretizations rapidly grows with the problem size and refinement level. These first results provide a strong motivation for future developments of micromagnetic solvers in TT format which could transcend the limitations of traditional simulators, with far reaching potential impacts on fundamental research and technology development.

AI.tldr: Tensor-train (TT) compression applied to 3D micromagnetic data exploits spatial sparsity (thin high‑gradient regions vs large uniform domains) to drastically reduce representation complexity: parameter count scales ≈ L^{1.8} and (1/a)^{1.2} instead of cubic, motivating TT-based micromagnetic solvers.
AI.method: Direct tensor‑train (TT) decomposition of discretized magnetization fields for representative flux‑closure configurations in soft‑magnetic rectangular prisms (near‑micrometer regime); empirical measurement of TT parameter‑count scaling with object size L and discretization scale a while controlling accuracy.
AI.tags: micromagnetics,tensor-train,sparse_representation,computational_magnetism,flux_closure,numerical_scaling,low-rank_tensor

title: Deep Strong light-matter Coupling in 3D Kane Fermions
summary: Deep strong light-matter coupling represents an extreme non-perturbative regime of quantum electrodynamics, in which the interaction strength exceeds the bare frequencies of the uncoupled systems. The ground state features strong quantum correlations between photons and matter excitations, and new cavity-driven phase transitions are expected to occur. Whether a superradiant quantum phase transition, marked by spontaneous dipole ordering and photon condensation, is possible has remained a long-standing and controversial question. Such phenomena have been proposed to arise in exotic electronic systems hosting Dirac and Kane fermions, owing to the formal absence of an $A^2$ term in their low-energy Hamiltonian. Here we exploit the ultralow effective mass of Kane fermions to realise Landau polaritons in a bulk mercury cadmium telluride layer coupled to a Fabry-Perot resonator. Using thermally tunable carrier density, we continuously tune the coupling from the weak to the deep-strong regime, achieving a record normalised coupling ratio exceeding 1.6 above room temperature. The measured polariton spectra are in excellent agreement with a rigorous, gauge-invariant microscopic theory. Despite the nonlinear Landau level structure of relativistic Kane fermions, we show that a diamagnetic $A^2$ term naturally emerges and precludes a superradiant phase transition. These results resolve the long-standing controversy surrounding cavity quantum electrodynamics of relativistic-like matter systems, extend deep-strong-coupling physics to Kane fermions, and open new opportunities for polaritonic semiconductor devices operating in extreme light-matter coupling regimes.

AI.tldr: Experimental demonstration of Landau polaritons in a bulk HgCdTe (Kane-fermion) layer strongly coupled to a Fabry–Pérot resonator; tuning carrier density drives the system from weak to deep-strong coupling (normalized g/ω>1.6) and measured spectra agree with a gauge-invariant microscopic theory that shows an emergent diamagnetic A^2 term prevents a superradiant phase transition.
AI.method: Fabrication and optical spectroscopy of a bulk mercury–cadmium–telluride layer embedded in a Fabry–Pérot cavity with thermally tunable carrier density to vary light–matter coupling; analysis via a rigorous, gauge-invariant microscopic cavity QED theory to fit polariton spectra and identify the emergent A^2 diamagnetic contribution.
AI.tags: quantum_devices, cavity_QED, deep_strong_coupling, Kane_fermions, Landau_polaritons, diamagnetic_A2, superradiant_phase

title: g-tensor Optimization in Ge/SiGe Quantum Dots
summary: Planar germanium heterostructures hosting hole-spin qubits are among the leading platforms for scalable semiconductor-based quantum computing. Yet, device performance is hindered by significant quantum dot variability, which leads to uncertainty in qubit energy levels and random orientations of the spin quantization axis. Tailored control of the g-tensor offers a strategy to overcome these limitations and achieve more reliable qubit operations. Here, we introduce a flexible optimization framework for engineering g-tensor properties. As a benchmark, we numerically obtain the optimal reshaping of the out-of-plane potential in a SiGe-Ge-SiGe quantum well to suppress the in-plane g-tensor components and realize the recently proposed gapless single-spin qubit encoding. This reshaping is achieved through heterostructure engineering, specifically by adjusting the silicon concentration within the quantum well, though the framework remains readily adaptable to alternative design objectives. Our results provide practical design principles for improving the tunability of the spin response, paving the way towards large-scale germanium-based quantum computers.

AI.tldr: They present a flexible numerical optimization framework to engineer the hole g-tensor in planar SiGe–Ge–SiGe heterostructures. As a benchmark, they find an optimal reshaping of the out-of-plane potential (via adjusting Si concentration in the quantum well) that suppresses in-plane g-tensor components and implements a gapless single-spin qubit encoding, offering practical design rules to improve tunability of Ge-based spin qubits.
AI.method: Numerical optimization of the heterostructure (out-of-plane potential) to tailor g-tensor properties; benchmarked by modeling a SiGe–Ge–SiGe quantum well and varying silicon concentration to minimize in-plane g-tensor components and realize a gapless single-spin encoding.
AI.tags: quantum_devices, quantum_computing, quantum_geometry, heterostructure_engineering, g-tensor, germanium, hole_spin_qubits

title: Giant Spin Magnetization from Quantum Geometry in Altermagnets
summary: Altermagnets host spin-split band structures while exhibiting vanishing equilibrium spin magnetization, making field-induced responses a direct probe of their quantum geometry. A central question, in this regard, is which quantum-geometric mechanism can generate a linear spin magnetization in centrosymmetric systems. Here we develop a unified framework based on a generalized quantum geometric tensor that incorporates both momentum translations and spin rotations of Bloch states, and decompose spin magnetization into equilibrium, electric-field-driven, and magnetic-field-driven contributions. We show that inversion symmetry forbids the linear electric-field response in centrosymmetric systems, while $C_n T$ symmetry further suppresses the equilibrium contribution in altermagnets. Consequently, centrosymmetric altermagnets provide a particularly clean realization in which the magnetic-field-induced spin magnetization emerges as the only symmetry-allowed linear quantum-geometric response. We demonstrate that this contribution originates entirely from the spin-rotation quantum metric, establishing it as the sole linear quantum-geometric mechanism in such systems. Using representative centrosymmetric altermagnets, including the $d$-wave compound $\mathrm{FeSb}_2$ and the $g$-wave compound $\mathrm{CrSb}$, we show that the spin-rotation quantum metric directly controls this response. Crucially, we predict a giant linear spin magnetization of order $10^{-2}μ_B\,\mathrm{nm}^{-3}$ at magnetic fields of $\sim 10\,\mathrm{mT}$, exceeding typical experimental values for conventional magnets by several orders of magnitude. Our results identify a universal quantum geometric mechanism of spin magnetization operative in centrosymmetric systems in general, and establish centrosymmetric altermagnets as an ideal platform for its experimental detection with potential applications in spintronics.

AI.tldr: The authors develop a unified quantum-geometric framework showing that in centrosymmetric altermagnets inversion and C_nT symmetries forbid linear electric-field and equilibrium spin responses, leaving a magnetic-field-induced linear spin magnetization as the sole symmetry-allowed effect. This response arises entirely from a spin-rotation quantum metric and is predicted to be giant (~10^{-2} μB nm^{-3} at ~10 mT) in representative materials (FeSb_2, CrSb).
AI.method: Analytical development of a generalized quantum geometric tensor that includes momentum translations and spin rotations of Bloch states, symmetry analysis (inversion and C_nT) to decompose spin magnetization into equilibrium, electric-field-driven, and magnetic-field-driven parts, and material-specific calculations for centrosymmetric altermagnets (d-wave FeSb_2 and g-wave CrSb) to compute the spin-rotation quantum metric and quantify the predicted response.
AI.tags: quantum_geometry, altermagnetic, magnetic_field_response, spin_rotation_quantum_metric, centrosymmetric, spintronics, FeSb2, CrSb

title: Observation of the Magnus Nonlinear Hall effect from Chiral Weyl Monopoles
summary: The nonlinear Hall effect (NLHE) connects crystalline symmetry to quantum geometry, offering a probe of band topology beyond linear transport. While most studies have focused on the Berry curvature dipole in low-symmetry crystals, mechanisms that directly probe Berry monopoles in higher-symmetry chiral lattices remain unexplored. Here, we report the observations of the NLHE in the chiral Weyl semimetal CoSi, a platform where the Berry curvature dipole is symmetry-forbidden. By employing focused ion beam-fabricated crossbar devices, we detect a robust second-harmonic Hall voltage under zero magnetic field, hosting all key signatures of the NLHE. Theoretical analysis attributes the nonlinear Hall conductivity to skew scattering of self-rotating electron wave packets, whose chirality is dictated by the underlying band topology, a process reminiscent of the classical Magnus effect. Furthermore, the NLHE signal exhibits a temperature-dependent sign reversal, and a strong, linearly field-dependent modulation that grows with carrier mobility, directly reflecting the topological Weyl nodes distribution near the Fermi level. These findings establish CoSi as a platform for Berry monopole-driven nonlinear transport, demonstrating a skew-scattering route to topological nonlinear Hall responses that bypasses conventional symmetry constraints.

AI.tldr: Observation of a zero-field nonlinear Hall effect in the chiral Weyl semimetal CoSi, where conventional Berry-curvature-dipole mechanisms are symmetry-forbidden; the signal is attributed to skew scattering of self-rotating (chiral) electron wave packets tied to Berry monopoles and shows temperature-dependent sign reversal and mobility-sensitive, linear field modulation.
AI.method: Experimental transport in focused-ion-beam fabricated crossbar devices measuring second-harmonic Hall voltage at zero magnetic field, combined with theoretical analysis that models nonlinear Hall conductivity arising from skew scattering of self-rotating electron wave packets (Berry-monopole–dictated chirality).
AI.tags: quantum_geometry, topology, Weyl_semimetal, nonlinear_Hall_effect, Berry_monopole, skew_scattering, transport_experiment, quantum_devices

title: Intrinsic anomalous thermal hall effect as a signature of quantum metric in d-wave altermagnets
summary: We investigate the intrinsic anomalous thermal Hall effect in d-wave altermagnets, where a transverse heat current is generated by a longitudinal temperature gradient in the absence of a magnetic field, with the leading response proportional to $(\nabla T)^3$. In these systems, the intrinsic Berry curvature-driven linear and thermal quantum-metric-driven second-order anomalous thermal Hall currents vanish as a consequence of crystalline symmetry. We show that the first nonvanishing contribution arises at third order in the temperature gradient and is governed by a nonlinear thermal Berry-connection polarizability, a quantity introduced in this work. Our analysis reveals a distinctive angular dependence of the anomalous thermal Hall conductance as the applied thermal gradient is rotated with respect to the crystal axes. We also find characteristic temperature and chemical-potential dependences that can be tested experimentally. These results identify unique quantum geometry-induced thermal responses and establish altermagnets as a promising platform for exploring intrinsic (i.e., scattering-time-independent) geometric transport phenomena.

AI.tldr: The paper predicts an intrinsic, scattering-time-independent anomalous thermal Hall effect in d-wave altermagnets that appears only at third order in the temperature gradient (∝(∇T)^3). Linear and second-order geometric contributions vanish by crystalline symmetry; the leading response is governed by a newly introduced nonlinear thermal Berry-connection polarizability and shows distinctive angular, temperature and chemical-potential dependencies.
AI.method: Symmetry and quantum-geometric analysis of d-wave altermagnets, deriving nonlinear thermal transport coefficients; introduction and calculation of a nonlinear thermal Berry-connection polarizability to obtain the third-order (in ∇T) intrinsic anomalous thermal Hall conductance, including angular and thermodynamic (T, μ) dependences.
AI.tags: altermagnetic, quantum_geometry, nonlinear_thermal_response, anomalous_thermal_hall, Berry_curvature, Berry_connection_polarizability, intrinsic_transport, topology
